transcript.content: Hi, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you in?

Well… the main thing is my sleep. It’s just gotten completely unmoored, I guess is the best way to put it. At first I’d sleep maybe two or three hours and then I’d be up, wide awake, drafting plans, making lists, feeling like I was ready to go, like the day had already started and I didn’t really need rest.

But now it’s different and worse. I’m lying awake before dawn, and my stomach is tight, and I don’t feel rested at all. It’s like my body won’t settle, but I’m not getting anything useful out of being awake either. It’s been wearing me down, and that’s really what made me come in.
During those nights when you slept only a few hours and still felt ready to go, did you feel unusually energized or euphoric?

Yes… yes, I did. At the time I would’ve called it “clear-headed” or “finally myself,” but looking back it was more than that. For weeks I felt almost brilliantly optimistic, like every problem had an obvious solution and every obstacle was just… trivial, like people were making everything harder than it needed to be.

And I wasn’t just cheerful. It had an edge to it. If someone questioned me—my judgment, my plans, even just slowed me down—I would snap. I’d feel like they were deliberately getting in the way, like they were trying to sabotage me, when in my mind I was the only sensible person in the room. It’s embarrassing to say that out loud, but that’s how it felt.
During that high-energy period, did your behavior cause serious problems in your life?

Yes. I think I wanted to tell myself it was just me being productive, but it did start to really interfere with things.

My wife has basically had to step in and take over the finances, which is… hard to admit, because I’ve always handled that sort of thing. Bills, accounts, donations, all of it. But she didn’t trust me to manage it safely anymore, and honestly I can see why now, even if at the time I was furious about it. She’s also been staying close to me, not really leaving me on my own much, because she’s worried about my safety and what I might do if I get carried away.

And I’ve stopped being reliable with the things that used to structure my life. I’m retired, but I’m involved with the museum and the arts council, and I have friends I usually see or keep up with. During that period, I just… stopped showing up consistently. I’d miss things, or say I was coming and then not go, or get so wrapped up in my own plans that I treated those commitments like they were beneath me. People have noticed. My wife has noticed. I’ve noticed now, though I didn’t want to at the time. So yes, it has caused real problems.
During that high-energy period, did you believe things that other people said were not true?

Yes. I mean… not things like hearing voices or believing something impossible was happening, but I did believe things about myself and my abilities that other people kept telling me were completely unrealistic.

I truly thought I could fix everything. My retirement accounts, for one—I was convinced I could repair the damage and somehow outthink the market, as if I suddenly had this special insight. And I was talking as if I could advise three start-ups at once, like these younger business people just needed my guidance and I could see the whole chessboard better than they could.

And with the arts council, I was absolutely certain I could turn it into some kind of regional powerhouse. Not just improve it a little—really transform it. I remember thinking everyone else had been thinking too small for years, and that my judgment was just… superior, frankly. At the time it didn’t feel arrogant to me. It felt obvious. Now, saying it out loud, it sounds grandiose and embarrassing, but yes—people told me I was not being realistic, and I didn’t believe them.
Have you ever had a period lasting at least two weeks when you felt depressed most of the day nearly every day?

Yes. Definitely longer than two weeks. It’s been… I’d say about nine months now, really, since all those plans fell apart. Since then I’ve been low most days, and it’s not just an occasional bad morning or feeling disappointed for a week. It’s been this long stretch of guilt and pulling away from things.

I keep thinking it should have lifted by now, or that I should be able to sort of shake myself out of it, but it hasn’t worked that way. It’s been there day after day, most of the day, for months.
Have you had thoughts that life isn’t worth living, or thoughts of killing yourself?

Yes… I’m ashamed to say that, but yes. There have been mornings when I wake up and the first thought is not that I want to start the day, but that it would have been easier if I just hadn’t woken up at all. Not in a dramatic way, exactly—more like this heavy feeling that everyone might be better off if I simply wasn’t here to keep causing trouble or needing looking after.

And it scared me. I don’t like admitting that, because I’ve always thought of myself as someone who can manage things, but I frightened myself enough that I told my wife I didn’t think I should be left alone. I said it out loud to her because I didn’t trust keeping it to myself. So yes, I’ve had those thoughts.
